nary_nodes.label: Europe's extreme summer heat
evidence: Temperatures in Europe hit a new high this summer, with hotter early-summer heatwaves triggering illness, deaths and the collapse of infrastructure across the continent.
Transport buckled on Sunday as temperatures hit 40C (104F) across Germany, the Czech Republic and Poland.
In France, days averaging 29.8C (85.6F) – spiking to 44C (111.2F) in one town – gave way to storms, leaving an estimated 1,000 excess deaths behind.

nary_nodes.label: Last summer's heatwave
evidence: Last summer’s heatwave alone caused an estimated 2,300 climate-related deaths in 12 European countries, WWA says.

nary_nodes.label: Europe's warming trend
evidence: Europe has warmed at roughly twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Commission’s climate change service, Copernicus.

And because Europe is warming roughly twice as fast as the rest of the planet, that gap with the global average is projected to keep widening – meaning whatever the world experiences on average in the coming decades, Europe will likely see first, and worse.

nary_nodes.label: Alpine glacier loss
evidence: Copernicus’s European State of the Climate 2025 report confirms this: more than 95 percent of the continent saw above-average annual temperatures last year, alongside record Alpine glacier loss and the highest sea-surface temperatures ever measured in Europe.
Alpine glaciers, which feed major European rivers, she says, have already shrunk past the point of recovery, and their contribution to summer river flow is “permanently reduced”.

nary_nodes.label: Heat-related deaths
evidence: The Lancet Countdown Europe calculates that there were 62,000 heat-related deaths across the region in 2024 alone, with projections showing a steep further rise by 2050 if we don’t make changes.
Deaths have already risen by an average of 52 per million people annually since the 1990s, he told Al Jazeera – a trend he says shows little sign of reversing on its own.

nary_nodes.label: Infrastructure collapse
evidence: Transport buckled on Sunday as temperatures hit 40C (104F) across Germany, the Czech Republic and Poland.

nary_nodes.label: Heatwaves more likely now
evidence: A study by World Weather Attribution (WWA) has found that intense heat on this level is now tens to hundreds of times more likely than it was in 2003, and was unheard of 50 years ago.

nary_nodes.label: Heat mortality to persist
evidence: “Heat-related mortality is likely to remain a feature of Europe’s warming climate,” warns Dr Hans Kluge, the World Health Organization (WHO)’s regional director for Europe.

nary_nodes.label: New normal for summers
evidence: Yes, it certainly looks that way. According to WWA, heatwaves were generally about 3.5C cooler in June 1976, and 2C cooler even in 2003.

nary_nodes.label: Global warming as cause
evidence: “Think of it like a race where the starting line has been moved much closer to the finish,” Dr Akshay Deoras of the University of Reading told Al Jazeera. Ultimately, this is down to global warming, he says.

nary_nodes.label: Extremes every couple decades
evidence: WWA’s modelling goes further: at current emissions rates, an event of the magnitude of this summer’s heatwave is expected to occur every couple of decades – and today’s extremes are effectively a preview of what an ordinary summer could look like by the middle of the century.

nary_nodes.label: Past emissions cause warming
evidence: Professor Hannah Cloke of the University of Reading told Al Jazeera that’s because the warming behind new, extreme weather patterns comes from emissions released decades ago, and the climate system takes time to respond – so we’re feeling the effects now of pollution from the past.

nary_nodes.label: Some damage permanent
evidence: Partly. Some of the damage is permanent. Some of it isn’t – yet.
Because the effects of pollution from decades ago are cumulative, “some of what we are experiencing this summer is already locked in”, Cloke says.

nary_nodes.label: Emissions reduction changes odds
evidence: “Every tonne of emissions avoided changes the odds of what comes next,” Cloke says.

nary_nodes.label: Housing stock unsuitable
evidence: “Most of the housing stock across this region was designed for a colder climate – to retain heat, not shed it,” he said, warning that without large-scale retrofitting, deaths could keep climbing past 2050 regardless of how good warning systems become.

nary_nodes.label: Plan for heat like flu
evidence: “Governments need to plan for heat the way they plan for winter flu – as a recurring, predictable challenge requiring permanent infrastructure, not a one-off crisis requiring emergency improvisation.”

nary_nodes.label: Priorities: warnings and water
evidence: Cloke points to two priorities: early warning systems that reliably reach the people who most need to be protected, and an overhaul of water infrastructure in Europe which has been built for rainfall patterns that no longer exist.

nary_nodes.label: Emissions cuts reduce heatwaves
evidence: Deoras says emissions also still matter: cutting them won’t eliminate heatwaves, which are “a natural part of the climate system”, but doing so would make them “less intense, less frequent and shorter-lived”.

nary_nodes.label: Window narrowing
evidence: They do warn that the window of opportunity for addressing the issue is narrowing: infrastructure can still be retrofitted, emissions can still be cut, warning systems can still be improved – if the decisions to do so are made now, rather than after the next heatwave.

type_definitions.definition: A large continuous landmass, typically one of the seven major divisions of the Earth's surface.
A nation with its own government, occupying a particular territory.
An organization that conducts scientific research and analysis.
An individual human being.
An organization with international membership, scope, or presence.
An institution of higher education and research which awards academic degrees.
An organization or agency that is part of a government.
A service that provides climate data, analysis, and projections.
A slowly moving mass of ice formed by the accumulation and compaction of snow.
A coordinated program or project aimed at conducting research on a specific topic.
An organization that gathers and disseminates news and information.
A span of time with a start and end, such as a season or a year.
A day of the seven-day week, such as Sunday or Monday.
A period of 365 days (or 366 in a leap year) starting from January 1st.
A unit of time corresponding to one of the twelve divisions of the year.
A period of ten years.
A collection of countries considered together, often for analysis or comparison.
An observable atmospheric event or condition, such as a heat dome or storm.
A long-term pattern or change in weather conditions, such as global warming.
A substance or agent that contaminates the environment, such as greenhouse gas emissions.
A material or source of supply found in nature, such as water or minerals.
The basic physical and organizational structures needed for the operation of a society, such as buildings and water systems.
A set of connected things or parts forming a complex whole, such as an early warning system.
A segment of the population defined by characteristics such as age, living situation, or other social factors.
A natural or artificial feature of the Earth's surface, such as a river or mountain.

Indicates the time period during which an event happened.
Indicates that an event or action had an impact on an entity.
Indicates that one event or action brought about another event or outcome.

Indicates that an entity or phenomenon is quantified or assessed by a particular instrument or organization.
Indicates that an entity or event is described or documented by a source.
Indicates that an event or condition is the result of a particular cause.
Indicates that a numerical value or statistic is derived by a particular entity.
Indicates that a value or trend is forecast to increase by a certain amount or time.
Indicates that a study, report, or finding is issued by a particular entity.
Indicates that a statement or event is about or relates to a particular subject.
Indicates that one entity is being compared with another, often in terms of magnitude or likelihood.
Indicates that a claim or opinion is expressed by a particular source.
Indicates that an individual is associated with an organization or institution.
Indicates that an entity or action includes or entails another entity.
Indicates that an entity or event has an influence on another entity.
Indicates that a water source supplies water to a river or other body of water.
Indicates that a reduction in size or extent is caused by a particular factor.
Indicates that an entity has the potential to return to a normal or healthy state.
Indicates that an entity is vulnerable to a particular threat or danger.
Indicates that an organization or service is run or managed by a particular entity.
